What is the difference between the JVM specification and HotSpot?

The JVM Specification defines the class file format, instruction set and required behaviour. It doesn't dictate memory layout or GC. HotSpot is the main implementation, used by OpenJDK and Oracle JDK. Others include OpenJ9 and the GraalVM compiler stack. So "Metaspace", "TLAB" and "G1" are HotSpot details, not language rules. Being able to separate "the spec says" from "HotSpot does" is a good sign in a senior interview.
Why does Java use both an interpreter and a JIT, instead of compiling everything ahead of time?

An interpreter starts immediately. Compiling everything would slow startup and waste effort on rarely run code. The JIT compiles only hot code, and it does this with knowledge unavailable to a static compiler: real branch frequencies and receiver types. It can then apply speculative inlining, with deoptimization to recover if an assumption fails. The cost is warm-up time and extra CPU early in the process's life. AOT approaches such as native image reverse that trade-off.
What does javap -c show and when have you needed it?

It disassembles a class file into bytecode. Uses: seeing how a language feature really compiles (i = i++, try-with-resources, string concat, switch on string), confirming whether a class was built with the expected version (javap -v shows the major version), and checking a library's actual method signature during a NoSuchMethodError.

It prints 5. The bytecode loads i (5) to the operand stack, increments the local to 6, and stores the value from the stack back into the local, overwriting 6 with 5. See the inc listing above, where istore_1 does this.

Explain the parent delegation model and how to break it, and why you might.

A loader asks its parent first and searches its own locations only if the parent fails. This protects core classes and prevents duplicates. To break it, a loader overrides loadClass and looks locally first. Tomcat does that so each web app can have its own library versions, while still delegating java.* and the Servlet API, since those must be shared. ServiceLoader is the other common exception: bootstrap-loaded code uses the thread context class loader to reach "down" to application classes.
Can I write my own java.lang.String and have it loaded?

No. With delegation the bootstrap loader's version wins, and the class path copy is never used. A custom loader that tries to define it gets SecurityException: Prohibited package name: java.lang. On Java 9 and later a class path copy of a package in java.base is also ignored, because that package belongs to a named module. Only special flags like --patch-module can replace JDK classes.
ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError?

ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception. It's thrown when code explicitly asks to load a class by name and it isn't found. NoClassDefFoundError is an Error: code compiled against a class, and the JVM can't provide it when it's needed. It has two causes: the class file is really missing at run time (for instance a provided dependency that isn't provided), or its static initializer failed earlier. The message Could not initialize class tells you it's the second.
What causes NoSuchMethodError in a Spring Boot app after a dependency upgrade?

A class compiled against library version X, and at run time another version without that method was chosen. Usually Maven's nearest-wins mediation picked an older transitive version. Steps: identify the owning class, find which JAR it came from with -Xlog:class+load or Foo.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource(), run mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose -Dincludes=group:artifact, then pin the version in dependencyManagement, or better use a BOM so related libraries move together.
How can a class be unloaded? Why did my Metaspace grow with each redeploy?

Classes unload only when their defining loader becomes unreachable, after no instance or Class reference remains. In a redeploy, the container discards the old loader. If anything outside the app holds an object from it, the loader survives along with all of its classes. Common holders are a ThreadLocal value on a pool thread owned by the container, a driver in DriverManager, a logging framework reference, a timer thread, and a shutdown hook. In a heap dump, find WebappClassLoader instances, look for one marked as stopped, and use Path to GC Roots.
Where are static variables stored? Where is the string pool?

In HotSpot since Java 7, static fields live on the heap, alongside the class's java.lang.Class mirror. The string table is a native structure, but the String objects it refers to have been on the heap since Java 7. Metaspace holds metadata only. Many tutorials still say "statics are in Metaspace", which is a mix-up between the spec's "method area" concept and HotSpot's implementation.
Stack vs heap: what goes where? Does an object ever live on the stack?

Primitive locals and references live in the frame. Objects, including their primitive fields, live on the heap, as do arrays. The language gives no way to request stack allocation. HotSpot's C2 can eliminate an allocation through scalar replacement if escape analysis proves the object doesn't escape, but that isn't a guarantee and it applies only to compiled code.
What is a TLAB and why does it matter?

A Thread-Local Allocation Buffer is a chunk of Eden owned by one thread, so allocation is a pointer bump with no synchronization. That's why Java allocation is often cheaper than malloc. Consequences: many threads can allocate without contention; objects allocated together by one thread sit together in memory, which is good for cache; and short-lived small objects are close to free, though each still adds to GC frequency.
How much memory does an Integer take vs an int? What about a String holding "abc"?

int: 4 bytes. Integer: 16 bytes for the object, plus a 4-byte reference (with compressed oops) to reach it. A String object is 24 bytes, plus its byte[]: 16 byte header + 3 bytes, rounded to 24. So 48 bytes for "abc". Compact strings (Java 9, JEP 254) store Latin-1 text with 1 byte per character; before that it was a char[] with 2 bytes each. A HashMap.Node adds more per entry on top. This is why a million-entry map of small objects can use hundreds of MB.
What are compressed oops, and why is a 40 GB heap possibly worse than a 31 GB heap?

Compressed oops store references in 32 bits, shifted by 3 because objects are 8-byte aligned, which addresses 32 GB. Beyond that limit the JVM switches to 64-bit references. References take 4 extra bytes each, and on a reference-heavy object graph that can consume all the extra capacity, and cache efficiency falls too. Check with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal | grep UseCompressedOops. Note that UseCompressedClassPointers is a separate feature.
What is the identity hash code, and is it the memory address?

No. Object.hashCode(), if not overridden, generates a number on first call (by default a thread-local random generator) and stores it in the mark word. That storage is why the value stays the same even as the GC moves the object. Moving objects is exactly why it can't be the address. The default toString()'s hex value is this hash, not an address.
Explain tiered compilation, OSR, and how you would see JIT activity.

Code starts in the interpreter (level 0), then C1 with profiling (level 3), and hot code reaches C2 (level 4). OSR switches a long-running loop to compiled code mid-execution. -XX:+PrintCompilation logs each compile, showing the tier, with % marking OSR and made not entrant marking invalidated code. Better tools are JFR compilation events and jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache. -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 forces C1 only, which is handy for short tools.
What is escape analysis? Does it really allocate objects on the stack?

Escape analysis determines how far an object's reference can travel: not at all, through a call as an argument, or globally. In HotSpot's C2, an object that doesn't escape can be scalar-replaced: its fields become plain local values and there's no allocation. Locks on it are also removed. It's not literally stack allocation. It only works after inlining, so a call that isn't inlined can make the object appear to escape. It can be disabled with -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis to measure its effect.
Why can adding one more interface implementation make hot code slower?

The JIT inlines call sites with one or two observed receiver types. If a third type shows up at a call site, it becomes megamorphic and stops being inlined, losing not just the call but all the optimizations inlining enabled. Loading a second implementation may also invalidate Class Hierarchy Analysis, deoptimizing code that assumed only one. That's the mechanism behind occasional performance surprises from "harmless" abstractions.
What is deoptimization, and when does it happen?

Compiled code is built on assumptions. When one fails, the JVM discards the compiled method and continues in the interpreter, rebuilding the frame. Triggers: reaching an uncommon trap (a branch never seen in profiling), a type check failing at an inlined site, or a newly loaded class invalidating a Class Hierarchy Analysis assumption. It's a normal mechanism. It's a problem only if a method repeatedly compiles and deoptimizes.
How does the GC deal with cycles? Why not use reference counting?

Tracing starts at GC roots, and anything not reached is garbage, whether or not it's in a cycle. Reference counting can't reclaim cycles without extra work, and it adds an atomic counter update to every reference assignment, which is costly under concurrency.
Explain what a minor GC does, step by step.

- Allocation fails because Eden is full, so a safepoint is requested.
- Roots are found: thread stacks, statics, and dirty cards or remembered sets from Old to Young.
- Live objects in Eden and the from-survivor space are copied to the to-survivor space, ages are incremented, and old enough objects are promoted to Old.
- References are updated, Eden and the from-space are considered empty, and survivor roles swap.
- Threads resume with empty Eden.
Its cost depends on the number of live objects, not on how many died. A larger young generation therefore doesn't necessarily mean longer pauses.
Why do we need card tables?

So a young collection doesn't need to scan all of Old for references into Young. A write barrier marks the card containing any object that has a reference stored into it, and the GC scans only dirty cards. Without this, minor GCs would cost as much as a full scan. G1's remembered sets are the region-based version of the same idea.
What is a safepoint? Why can a pause be long when GC work is short?

A safepoint is a state where all Java threads have stopped at known points, so the JVM can safely examine or change the heap. Threads reach one by checking a poll. If one thread takes a long time, for example in a long counted loop or a page fault, every other thread sits waiting. -Xlog:safepoint prints "Reaching safepoint" separately from "At safepoint". A long first number points at time to safepoint rather than the collector.
Difference between minor GC, major GC, mixed GC and full GC?

- Minor (young): collects Young.
- Major: loosely, collecting Old. The term is not precise, so ask which collector is meant.
- Mixed (G1): Young plus a selection of Old regions.
- Full: whole heap, usually long STW, a fallback under G1.
G1 vs Parallel vs ZGC: how would you choose?

Parallel: batch and data processing where total throughput counts and pauses of a second or more are fine. G1: the sensible default for services, balancing throughput and pause targets of around 100-200 ms. Generational ZGC: latency-critical services where p99.9 matters, with heaps from a few GB upward, and CPU headroom available. Serial: tiny containers and CLI tools. Measure rather than assume: a low-pause collector with too small a heap stalls allocation and gives worse results than G1.
Why was CMS removed?

CMS never compacted the old generation, so fragmentation eventually forced a long single-threaded full GC. It also had a high maintenance cost, a large tuning surface, and failure modes ("concurrent mode failure"). G1 replaced it for most uses, and it was deprecated in 9 (JEP 291) and removed in 14 (JEP 363).
How can ZGC move objects while threads are running?

A load barrier runs each time a reference is loaded from the heap. ZGC stores metadata bits in the pointer. If the pointer is out of date, the slow path finds the object's new location (or relocates it first), and overwrites the field with the good pointer. Application threads therefore help finish the GC's work. STW phases handle only small tasks such as root scanning preparation, so pause time doesn't scale with heap size.
Is System.gc() ever a good idea? What does it do on G1?

It's only a hint. On G1 it normally runs a full STW collection, unless -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent makes it start a concurrent cycle instead. So calling it in application code tends to create the pauses you're trying to avoid. Legitimate uses are limited to tests and benchmarks. A library that calls it can be found with the GC cause in the log: Pause Full (System.gc()).
Soft vs weak vs phantom references?

Soft: cleared under memory pressure, and all before an OOM. Weak: cleared at the next GC once only weakly reachable. Phantom: get() always returns null; you only learn from a queue that the object is gone, which makes it right for post-mortem cleanup, and it's what Cleaner is built on. WeakHashMap uses weak keys. ThreadLocalMap also has weak keys, with strong values.
Why is finalize() deprecated, and what replaces it?

It has no timing guarantee and might not run at all. It delays reclamation by at least one GC cycle, runs on a limited finalizer thread that can fall behind, has no ordering, allows objects to be resurrected, and adds a cost to allocating such objects. It was deprecated in 9 and deprecated for removal in 18 (JEP 421). Use try-with-resources for deterministic cleanup, and Cleaner as a safety net.
Why is ThreadLocal a classic memory leak in Tomcat?

Each thread has a ThreadLocalMap. Its entries hold the key weakly and the value strongly. Tomcat threads are pooled and live indefinitely, so a value set during a request stays until overwritten, even after the request ends. That leaks data between requests too, which can be a security problem, such as one user's context visible to another. And if the value's class came from a web app's loader, it pins the loader across redeploys. Always call remove() in finally.
Explain shallow vs retained size, and a dominator tree.

Shallow size is the memory of one object alone. Retained size is what would be freed if it were collected: everything reachable only through it. In a dominator tree, a node's children are objects it alone keeps alive. So a HashMap might have a shallow size of 48 bytes and a retained size of 2 GB, and the tree's top entries show where memory really goes.
Scenario: Heap climbs to the limit over two days, then the service dies with an OOM. Walk through it.

- Check GC logs: is the post-GC floor rising? That says leak rather than a burst.
- Restart to restore service. Make sure HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError is on, with a path on a volume that survives the restart.
- Analyze the dump in MAT. Leak Suspects, then dominator tree.
- Follow Path to GC Roots to see who holds it, such as a static cache or a queue.
- Check the code and recent commits. Reproduce it in a load test.
- Fix, then add a metric (cache size, or heap after GC through Micrometer) with an alert.
Scenario: p99 jumped after a release, but CPU and heap look normal. How do you investigate?

- Correlate first: compare latency graphs with GC pauses. If GC pauses line up with spikes, look at the GC log. Otherwise leave GC out of it.
- Check for lock contention and pool saturation: JFR's JavaMonitorEnter events, thread dumps, HikariCP pending connections.
- Check downstream timings using distributed tracing, as a downstream or SQL plan change is a common cause.
- Compare with the previous release: flame graphs from async-profiler or JFR show new hot paths. Look for new allocation, logging, or N+1 queries.
- Look at safepoint time and deoptimization.
The method: form a hypothesis from data, change one thing, and verify.
Scenario: The container is OOMKilled, but the heap is only 60% used. What's going on?

Heap use doesn't describe the process. The kernel's OOM killer uses the cgroup memory limit against RSS. Causes: too high a MaxRAMPercentage so the committed heap plus non-heap exceeds the limit; thread stacks from many threads; Netty or Kafka direct buffers; Metaspace without a limit; and native allocations from libraries, such as compression. Enable -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, and use jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary, comparing that with RSS. The difference shows memory outside the JVM's accounting. Then set heap percentage and MaxMetaspaceSize, cap direct memory, and add headroom. Exit code 137 and no Java exception are the giveaways.
Scenario: CPU is at 100% and GC logs show back-to-back full GCs. What now?

This is a "GC death spiral": the live set nearly fills the heap, each collection recovers almost nothing, and the application barely runs. Parallel GC would report GC overhead limit exceeded. Take a heap dump if possible (on an instance you've removed from the load balancer). The immediate relief is more heap or fewer requests. The cause is a leak, an unbounded in-memory result (like loading a whole table), or traffic beyond what the heap can hold. -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError doesn't help until the OOM is actually thrown, so a liveness check that depends on response time helps here.
Scenario: How do you diagnose high CPU on one Java process?

Start with GC: if GC threads are busy, it's memory pressure. Otherwise, use top -H -p <pid> to find hot threads, and match them to nid in jcmd <pid> Thread.print. Take several dumps. A better option is an async-profiler CPU flame graph or a JFR recording. Common causes: an infinite loop (historically HashMap under concurrent modification), regex backtracking, a spinning retry without backoff, and heavy serialization.
Scenario: Startup takes 45 seconds on Kubernetes and pods fail liveness probes. How do you approach this?

Use a startup probe rather than an excessive liveness delay. Then look at why it's slow: a CPU limit during startup is the most common reason, as class loading and JIT are CPU-heavy, so a higher startup CPU allowance helps. Check with -Xlog:class+load and Spring's ApplicationStartup or Actuator's startup endpoint. Options for reducing it: CDS or the AOT cache, lazy initialization where acceptable, fewer auto-configurations, or native image if the trade-offs fit.
What's in your standard production JVM flag set?

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
-Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20m
-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
Almost everything else stays at its default until a measurement justifies changing it. Size MaxMetaspaceSize from your own measurements; 256 MB is an example, not a recommendation.
What is CDS, and what's the difference between CDS, the AOT cache and native image?

CDS stores parsed class metadata in a mapped archive, so class loading is faster and memory can be shared. The AOT cache (Java 24 onward) builds on that, and also keeps classes loaded and linked, and from 25 method profiles too, while staying on a normal JVM with JIT and all Java dynamism. Native image compiles to a standalone binary, with no JVM, under a closed-world assumption. In short: CDS and AOT speed up the JVM, while native image replaces it.
What is the closed-world assumption in native image, and how does it affect Spring?

All code that can run must be known at build time, so classes can't be loaded at run time. Reflection, dynamic proxies, resources and serialization must be declared in metadata. Spring normally decides a lot at startup, such as evaluating @Conditional and creating proxies. Spring AOT moves that work to build time and generates source and hints. Consequences: the set of beans and profiles is fixed at build time, so @Profile can't change at run time as it does on the JVM, and libraries without metadata may need hints.
Why is a hand-written timing loop not a valid benchmark? What does JMH fix?

The first iterations run in the interpreter, then C1, then C2, so timings mix compilation stages. The JIT can hoist or delete work whose result is unused, fold constants, and inline differently than in production. GC can pause in the middle. JMH runs warm-up iterations, forks separate JVMs, consumes results via Blackhole, and reports error bars, so you compare steady-state performance.
After each deployment, the first minute of traffic has very high latency, then it settles. Why, and what can you do?

That is JVM warm-up: classes load lazily, code runs interpreted until the JIT compiles hot paths, and caches/connection pools are cold. Mitigations: a readiness probe that only passes after a warm-up routine has exercised the main endpoints; pre-initialised pools (Hikari minimumIdle); CDS or the AOT cache (newer JDKs can also store method profiles) to cut class loading and JIT time; gradual traffic shifting in the rollout; and enough CPU during startup, because CPU limits throttle the JIT compiler threads.
Can you catch OutOfMemoryError? Should you?

You can, because it is a Throwable, but you rarely should. It can be thrown in any allocation, possibly in another thread, leaving shared state half-updated, and the handler itself may fail to allocate. A narrow exception: catching it around one large, isolated allocation (e.g. a huge image buffer) to reject that request. In services, prefer -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError plus -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so the orchestrator restarts a clean instance and you keep a dump for analysis.
-Xmx vs -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize vs -Xss vs -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize: what does each limit, and what happens when you hit it?

Flag | Limits | Default | When exceeded
-Xmx | Java heap | 25% of RAM or container limit | OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize | Class metadata | Unlimited | OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
-Xss | Each thread's stack | 1 MB on 64-bit Linux | StackOverflowError in that thread
-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize | NIO direct buffers | Same as max heap | OutOfMemoryError mentioning direct buffer memory
-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize | JIT-compiled code | 240 MB with tiered compilation | Warning "CodeCache is full", JIT stops, app gets slower
Interview tip: "unable to create native thread" is not about any of these limits. It means the OS or container refused another thread, often a thread leak. In containers, leave room for everything outside -Xmx.
Heap dump vs thread dump vs JFR recording vs GC log: which one answers your question?

| Heap dump | Thread dump | JFR recording | GC log
Answers | What is holding memory? | What is every thread doing right now? | Where did time, allocation and locking go over a period? | How long were pauses, how full was the heap?
Capture | jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump f.hprof | jcmd <pid> Thread.print | jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=r.jfr | -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log
Cost | Stop-the-world pause; file about the size of the used heap | Short pause | Low (about 1% with default settings) | Negligible
Read with | Eclipse MAT | Your eyes; take 3 a few seconds apart | JDK Mission Control | GCViewer or similar
Typical symptom | Leak, OOM | Hang, deadlock, pool exhaustion | High CPU, latency | GC pauses, heap trend
Interview tip: a heap dump contains every value in memory, including passwords, tokens and patient data. Treat it as sensitive: restrict access and delete it after analysis.
String.intern() vs G1 string deduplication vs compact strings?

| intern() | String deduplication | Compact strings
What it does | Returns one canonical String object from the string table | GC makes equal Strings share one backing byte[] | Stores Latin-1 text as 1 byte per char
Turned on by | Your code calling it | -XX:+UseStringDeduplication | On by default since Java 9
a == b afterwards | true | Still false: the String objects stay separate | Not affected
Cost | Table lookup on each call | Background GC work | None noticeable
Rule of thumb: do not intern by hand to save memory. If a heap dump shows many duplicate strings, try deduplication first; it needs no code change.
